newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka president, kin battle over poll violence.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka president, kin battle over poll violence.

text.p: A family war of words has cast a shadow over this month's local elections in Sri Lanka after President Chandrika Kumaratunga's estranged brother accused her of perpretating violence against his party's supporters.

Anura Bandaranaike, a lawmaker of the main opposition United National Party (UNP), charged Kumaratunga's People's Alliance (PA) government of violating election laws and unleashing a wave of terror ahead of the polls.
Bandaranaike said last week his party's candidates had been attacked and demanded an end to the harassment of his supporters in the family's traditional political stronghold of Gampaha district.
But Kumaratunga has denied the charges, saying the polls were being held in a peaceful manner and that the situation was calm in Gampaha district, just outside the capital Colombo.
Referring to her brother's allegations, she told India's The Hindu newspaper during the weekend that poll-related violence could be curtailed if the UNP reined in its unruly supporters.
The local elections, the first popularity test for Kumaratunga's coalition government, are scheduled for March 21.

"My parents ruled the country for seventeen years. They are still respected for their decent politics. Let not another Bandaranaike change all that," Bandaranaike was quoted as saying by the Island newspaper.

His father, S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike, was Sri Lanka's prime minister in the 1950s and his mother, Sirima Bandaranaike, was the world's first woman prime minister. She is now serving her third term as premier in her daughter's government.

The poll campaign has been marred by the killing of a ruling coalition lawmaker last month, sparking two days of riots in the legislator's constituency of Ratnapura, 80 km (50 miles) southeast of Colombo.
A UNP member of parliament and a former UNP mayor are among the suspects detained by police in connection with the killing.
The government has since launched a crackdown on illegal weapons used by politicians, granting an amnesty till March 15 for the surrender of illegal firearms.

Politicians and activists in Sri Lanka own a large number of guns, many of them unlicenced, which they obtained in the late 1980s to protect against insurgent groups and the Tamil Tiger rebels, who are fighting a separatist war in the island's north and east.

Kumaratunga told The Hindu newspaper that since most of the weapons were given to politicians when the UNP was in power, the opposition party was best placed to give information on these arms and to ensure their surrender.
But Bandaranaike has said that even Kumaratunga's Sri Lanka Freedom Party (SLFP), the main constituent of the PA, had also received arms, which the PA had not disclosed.
Bandaranaike was quoted as saying by The Island newspaper on Monday that he himself had distributed the weapons to SLFP supporters when he was the party leader in late 1980s.
He quit the SLFP to join the UNP after a fight with his sister over party leadership before the 1994 general elections.

Bandaranaike, an ardent critic of the government and its policies, was at the centre of another crisis last September when the opposition threatened to stop cooperating with the PA over a proposed peace plan to end the separatist war, now in its 14th year.
An independent monitoring group said at the weekend a total of 944 incidents of election related violence have been reported since last month.
The highest number of allegations have been made against the PA, the Centre for Monitoring Election Violence said in a statement.
